Ecuador Oil Workers' Strike Disrupts Output, Threatens Exports

QUITO, June 10 – Oil and gas production in Ecuador has been severely disrupted after thousands of workers walked off the job on Monday in a strike over pay and working conditions, union and industry sources said.

The stoppage, which began at midnight, has led to the suspension of operations at several key oilfields and processing facilities across the Amazon region, according to officials from the National Federation of Oil and Gas Workers. "We have more than 4,000 workers participating in the strike. Our main demand is fair wages and improved safety standards," union leader Carlos Paredes said by phone. He added that negotiations with employers had stalled over the weekend.

The walkout has already forced major producers such as AndesPetrol and PetroAndina to halt or curtail operations at multiple sites, according to statements released by the companies. A spokesperson for AndesPetrol estimated that production at its Sacha and Shushufindi fields had dropped by 60 percent since the early hours of Monday, with only skeleton crews remaining to ensure environmental safety. "We are closely monitoring the situation and prioritizing the security of our installations," the spokesperson said.

The government’s Ministry of Energy confirmed the strike had reduced national crude output by an estimated 110,000 barrels per day, roughly 35 percent of Ecuador’s typical daily production. "We are making every effort to mediate between the parties and restore operations as soon as possible," Deputy Energy Minister Lucía Viteri said at a press conference. She warned that continued disruptions could impact the country’s export commitments.

Analysts said the strike is putting Ecuador’s oil sector under significant strain. "These disruptions come at a sensitive moment for the industry, as global demand remains volatile and Ecuador is highly dependent on oil revenues," said Juan Estrella, an energy analyst at Quito-based consultancy Grupo Horizonte.

The Ecuadorian Oil Producers Association called for a swift resolution, urging both sides to return to the bargaining table. "Every day of lost production is a blow not just to companies, but to the national economy," association president Diego Zamora said in a statement.

As of Monday afternoon, talks between union leaders and company representatives had yet to resume. Striking workers said they would remain off the job until their demands are met.

The strike is ongoing and its full impact on output and exports remains uncertain.
